title: STAND: Self-Aware Precondition Induction for Interactive Task Learning
topic: General Machine Learning->Online Learning, Active Learning and Bandits
claim: A standard tree commits to one split per node; ours expands multiple splits and bounds a general condition space by a specific extension.
layout: 2 regions: small tree left, large multi-branch graph right; top-to-bottom flow
description: The figure sets a conventional decision tree against the STAND structure, both fit to the same seven-sample binary table shown at the top. On the left, a small tree splits on X4, then X3, with colored edges. Its leaves carry sample lists and green check or red X badges. On the right, a much larger graph has nodes holding sample sets and several filled grey split circles per node. Thick colored lines (orange, green, blue, red, purple) run from the splits down to seven leaf nodes. Below the leaves, a grey band lists each leaf's specific extension as colored literals joined by AND. Grey boxes at the top show the derived condition sets (OR of literals) for the tree and for STAND. The dense, colorful right side draws the eye first.
caption: Decision tree and STAND fit to the same input data. In STAND, multiple splits (filled grey circles) are expanded per node. STAND builds a general condition space (top-right) that is bounded below by a specific extension (bottom).
abstract: In interactive task learning (ITL), AI agents learn new capabilities from limited human instruction provided during task execution. STAND is a new method of data-efficient rule precondition induction specifically designed for these human-in-the-loop training scenarios. A key feature of STAND is its self-awareness of its own learning -- it can provide accurate metrics of training progress back to users. STAND beats popular methods like XGBoost, decision trees, random forests, and version spaces at small-data precondition induction tasks, and is highly accurate at estimating when its performance improves on holdout examples. In our evaluations, we find that STAND shows more monotonic improvement than other models with low rates of error recurrence. These features of STAND support a more consistent training experience, enabling human instructors to estimate when they are finished training and providing active-learning support by identifying trouble spots where more training is required.
